content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"Every material assertion actually printed in the BOOK ENTRY is carried directly by the printed KJV excerpts. The core identification — the wall as Salvation, the covenant's enclosure God provides — is not an inference but a near-quotation: Isaiah 60:18 explicitly names the walls 'Salvation,' and Zechariah 2:5 supplies the substance ('I... will be unto her a wall of fire round about'), showing the wall is God Himself around His people. The two counterfeit assertions are equally explicit: Proverbs 18:11 gives wealth as 'an high wall in his own conceit' (self-built), and Ezekiel 13:10-15 gives the wall daubed with untempered mortar by those 'saying, Peace; and there was no peace,' which a stormy wind, shower, and hailstones flatten — precisely 'the whitewashed wall of false peace that the storm flattens.' The strongest genuine rival, the generic 'protection/security' reading dominant in the common interpretation, shares the same core referent and is merely broader and vaguer; it does not contradict the entry and in fact the entry explains the same texts more precisely, since Scripture itself names the wall 'Salvation' rather than leaving it as an unlabeled protection metaphor. The alternative 'dividing wall of hostility' reading (Eph 2:14) is a passage-specific application that cannot account for the printed texts (Isa 60:18; Zech 2:5; Prov 18:11; Ezek 13) at all. No supplied text is better explained by any counter than by the entry's core.","book_core_identification":"The wall symbolizes Salvation — the covenant's enclosure, God Himself as the protective boundary around His people ('thou shalt call thy walls Salvation'; alternatively, the New Testament's most iconic wall is the 'dividing wall of hostility' (Eph 2:14), a barrier of separation Christ abolishes.","counter_core_identification":"Wall = protection/security/defense generally (context-dependent), or in its NT-iconic use, a barrier of separation and hostility.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"SAME_CORE_BROADER","material_core_denial":"The generic protection reading does not deny the book's core; it agrees the wall is God-given security and merely declines to fix the label 'Salvation.' The separation/hostility reading, if pressed as the primary meaning, would deny that the wall symbolizes salvation, but it is passage-specific to Ephesians 2 and cannot account for the entry's printed texts.","counter_case":["Multiple genres use walls differently (Jericho's obstacle, Proverbs 25:28 self-control, Lamentations judgment), so a single fixed equation 'wall = salvation' may over-systematize a polyvalent image.","Ephesians 2:14 is the most theologically prominent NT wall, and there the wall is negative — a barrier removed — which the label 'Salvation' does not obviously fit.","Isaiah 60:18 could be a local poetic renaming rather than a standing symbolic definition."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Scripture itself supplies the label twice: 'thou shalt call thy walls shows the substance behind the masonry (God Himself as the wall), which unifies the protection intuition and the salvation label into one coherent identification: the covenant's enclosure is God around His people.","The entry's true/counterfeit polarity is textually exact: Prov 18:11 explicitly marks the rich man's high wall as existing 'in his own conceit,' and Ezek 13:10-15 explicitly marks
